pages.title: The operational case
pages.instruction: Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Venue manager · simulated source
pages.subject: A digital-first proposal
paragraphs: The venue manager proposes moving towards digital payment to simplify checkout and reduce cash handling. Staff currently reconcile different payment types at the end of each day. The manager expects a more consistent process, but has not supplied trial results showing faster service or lower total costs. Any transaction fees and equipment requirements would still need checking.

The proposal does not yet define a fallback for connection failure or a customer without a usable device. The manager is open to a trial and wants a recommendation that explains what the normal process should be, what happens when it fails and how staff would communicate an exception. This is a simulated operational perspective, not evidence that digital-only systems always work better.

pages.title: The access perspective
pages.instruction: Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Community account · simulated source
pages.subject: Participation and temporary failure
paragraphs: A community representative asks the venue to consider people who cannot reliably use its proposed digital process. That includes limited access to a suitable account or device, but also temporary problems such as a dead battery or an unavailable payment connection. A person who normally pays digitally may still need another route on a particular day.

The representative does not claim that cash resolves every access issue. They ask for a practical fallback, clear information about fees and privacy, and a process that does not require a customer to explain private circumstances publicly. Their concern is whether people can complete an ordinary purchase. The recommendation should address that need while recognising the venue’s operational aims, and specify what would make the proposed trial worth revising.

pages.title: Reach a balanced recommendation

pages.title: An ordinary user loses digital access
pages.instruction: Listen for the new information and decide how to respond
pages.message: Hi, Ana. I wanted to add an experience to the payment-policy discussion. I normally pay by card, but last week my phone battery died while I was out. At the next place, the payment connection also stopped working for a while. I had some cash with me, but their digital-only process didn’t allow it, so I couldn’t complete the purchase then. I’m not saying that one incident proves digital payment is always unreliable. It does show that temporary loss of access can affect people who usually use it comfortably. Could your recommendation say what happens in that situation, including how staff explain the fallback without embarrassing the customer? I’d also want to know whether a transaction fee changes between the normal process and the fallback. A policy can aim for convenience while still making a specific plan for the moment the convenient route fails

pages.title: Cashless payments: who receives the tip?
pages.instruction: Watch an archived report about pooled tips, then recommend a fair policy with conditions

video.title: Where do your tips go? — BBC Learning English

items.prompt: What payment change does the interviewee describe?
items.hint: Listen to how more tips are being paid
items.answer: More tips and service charges are being paid by card

items.prompt: What is the intended function of pooling those payments?
items.hint: Listen to the explanation of the shared arrangement
items.answer: The stated aim is to collect the tips and distribute them fairly

items.prompt: Does giving a payment to one worker guarantee that worker receives it all?
items.hint: Listen to the explanation after the interview
items.answer: No. The payment may be distributed across the business under its system

items.prompt: Recommend a tipping policy that considers both customers and workers
items.hint: Include transparency, an exception and a way to review it
items.answer: Example: The business should publish how tips are divided, offer a cash option where feasible and let staff challenge an unfair distribution
